clips.text: An artificial pacemaker senses cardiac electrical activity and can deliver timed electrical stimuli. The pulse generator contains the power source and circuitry. Leads connect it to electrodes in or on the heart, although leadless systems also exist. A pacing stimulus may appear as a narrow spike on the E C G, but modern spikes are not always easily visible. The device supports electrical timing; an electrical response still does not by itself prove an effective mechanical pulse.

clips.text: Transcutaneous pacing delivers stimuli through skin pads and is generally temporary. Temporary transvenous pacing uses a lead passed through a vein. Implanted systems provide longer-term support, with configurations chosen for the clinical problem. This module identifies devices and recording patterns only. It does not specify pad placement, current settings, thresholds, or programming steps. Those require equipment-specific training, current protocols, and clinical supervision.

clips.text: Pacing rate, output, and sensing are different settings. Sensing determines how the device detects intrinsic activity. Output relates to the delivered stimulus. In an inhibited demand mode, a sensed event can prevent an unnecessary pacing pulse. In an asynchronous mode, stimuli occur without responding to intrinsic events in the usual way. Triggered and dual-chamber behaviors follow particular timing rules; they are not simply a response to any missed or abnormal beat.

clips.text: Atrial pacing may show a stimulus followed by a P wave if atrial capture occurs. Ventricular pacing may show a stimulus followed by a paced Q R S, often wider with conventional ventricular pacing. Dual-chamber systems can sense and pace both chambers, but a strip does not always show two spikes on every cycle. Atrial-only pacing requires appropriate atrial tissue and atrioventricular conduction; it is not a standard solution for permanent atrial fibrillation.

clips.text: Cardiac resynchronization therapy coordinates ventricular activation in selected patients with ventricular dyssynchrony. Traditional biventricular systems stimulate right and left ventricular regions. The visible number or spacing of spikes alone does not establish correct resynchronization. Some newer pacing strategies activate the conduction system more directly. Device selection and programming are clinical decisions, while this study module focuses on recognizing the limits of what the surface recording can show.

clips.text: Electrical failure to capture means a pacing stimulus is not followed by the expected atrial or ventricular depolarization. Undersensing may produce stimuli despite intrinsic events; oversensing may inhibit needed pacing. Apparent failure to output requires context, including the programmed mode and rate, because the absence of a visible pacing spike does not necessarily indicate malfunction. Mechanical capture is a separate assessment. Do not diagnose device failure or change settings from spike position alone.
